title: The mandala offering
hookLine: offering the whole universe, pictured as a mandala of rice

lines: A PLATE, A BOWL OF RICE.
cards: A small round plate, often brass or silver. A bowl of rice beside it.

The practitioner wipes the plate in circles with the inside of the wrist, then lets rice fall in a ring, sets a smaller ring on top, then another, until there's a little stacked heap with an ornament on top.
A verse is recited. Then the rice is tipped off, the plate wiped, and it all begins again. From across the room it could pass for a child's game with dinner.
In the practitioner's mind, it's the whole universe, being given away.

teach.b: First, the word. Mandala is a Sanskrit word usually translated circle. Here the circle is the world itself, ordered and complete, seen from above.
Second, what the rice stands for.

The offering draws on a picture of the cosmos found in Buddhist texts from India: at the center a great mountain, Meru; around it continents and oceans, a sun and a moon, and every precious thing anyone could want.

Each heap of rice stands in for a part of that world, so the little plate holds mountains, oceans and everything between. Third, why give the universe away. None of it is yours, and that's partly the point.
Teachers explain the offering as a training in generosity with no ceiling.
People often give what they can spare; here the practitioner gives everything, beautiful things included, along with their own body and their own good deeds.
Tibetan teachers count it among the ways of gathering merit, the goodness that ripens into a path. What gets lighter is the grip. Fourth, wiping the plate.
Some teachers say the wiping is as much the practice as the heaping: clearing the mind the way you clear the plate. And when the rice is tipped off, nothing is kept.
In year one you met the sand mandala some monasteries build and sweep away. This one shares the word, but it's a gift you can carry in two hands.

how: In the Tibetan foundational practices, students build and offer a mandala of rice on a round plate many times while reciting an offering verse, picturing the whole universe given to the Buddha, the teaching and the community.

games.why: nothing is kept. the world is offered, emptied and offered again, and what gets lighter is the grip.

practice: Rest your hands open on your lap, palms up, and bring to mind one thing complete and good in your world: a morning, a view, a person's laugh, the light in a window.

Let it sit in your open hands the way the rice sits on the plate, then give it away, and let your hands stay open after. If you are a Buddhist, you can offer it to the Buddha, the teaching and the community.

orig.note: Sanskrit mandala: usually translated circle; here, the whole world pictured as one round offering.
